paragraphs.source_en: Unlike my master, I am naturally an early riser, and by this time I was already unbearably hungry. Being a cat, I could hardly expect to get breakfast before the people of the house had sat down to theirs; yet perhaps this is precisely the shallow nature of cats, for when I imagined a fragrant steam rising hot from the abalone shell that served as my dish, I could not sit still. When one pins hope on something one knows to be futile, the wisest course is to picture that hope in the mind and keep the body perfectly still. In practice, however, that is hard to do; one longs to test whether the heart's desire agrees with reality, and even when disappointment is plainly certain, one refuses to give up until that disappointment has been experienced in fact. Unable to endure it any longer, I crept into the kitchen. My first step was to peer into the abalone shell behind the stove to see whether my portion of soup was there; as expected, the empty shell I had licked clean the night before still sat there, shining in the autumn sunlight that leaked in through the skylight. The maid Osan was transferring the freshly cooked rice into the rice tub, then stirring the soup and vegetables in the pot set over the fire. Around the rim of the pot, boiled-over rice water had dried into many crackly streaks, some of them looking like thin sheets of Yoshino paper pasted on. Since both rice and soup were ready, I thought she might perfectly well let me eat. At such a time, politeness is pointless; even if I failed to get what I wanted, I would lose nothing, so I might as well boldly demand my breakfast, for though I am only a dependent cat in this household, hunger is hunger all the same. Having reached that decision, I meowed a few times at Osan, as if coaxing, as if appealing, as if airing my grievances; but Osan paid me no heed at all. I had long known that she was stubborn by nature and ignorant of human feeling, but that was where my skill came in: I had to cry in just the right way to awaken her sympathy. So I changed my meowing into a plaintive yowl, and I myself believed that this sorrowful cry carried a tragic note sufficient to wring the heart of any wanderer at the ends of the earth. Yet Osan remained utterly indifferent. Perhaps this woman was deaf. A deaf person could not serve as a maid, so most likely she was deaf only to the voices of cats. They say there are people in the world called color-blind; though the person himself believes he has perfectly normal sight, the doctor calls it a disability. This Osan is probably sound-blind. Sound-blindness, of course, must also count as a disability. Disabled though she may be, she is extremely overbearing; late at night, no matter how urgently I need to urinate and ask her to open the door, she has never once opened it for me. On the rare occasion she lets me out, she then absolutely refuses to let me back in. Even in summer, night dew is harmful to the body, to say nothing of the heavy frost of late autumn. To stand beneath the eaves all night waiting for sunrise, enduring such hardship, is more than ordinary people can possibly imagine.

paragraphs.source_zh: 和主人不同，我总要早起，此时我已经饿得受不了。以我们猫儿的身份，在家中诸人用餐之前，毕竟是不可能吃上早饭的，但是，这也许就是我们猫儿的浅薄之处吧，一想到在我吃饭用的鲍鱼壳里会热气腾腾地发出香喷喷的味道来，就坐立不安。明知道实现不了的事还要寄予希望的时候，最上策就是把希望在头脑里描绘一番，稳住身体不动。但实际上却很难做到，总想试验一下内心的愿望是否和实际相符，甚至还要试验一下明明注定是要失望的事，在实际体验到这种失望之前，还不肯罢休。我实在忍不住，便爬到厨房去。我第一步就是先瞧瞧放在灶后边的鲍鱼壳里是否有我的那份汤，结果不出所料，我昨晚舐得罄尽的鲍鱼空壳依然摆在那里，在从天窗漏进来的秋阳的照耀下，发着光亮。厨娘阿三正将新煮好的米饭移到饭桶里去，然后又去搅拌架在火上锅里的汤菜。在锅边上流出煮沸的米汤，烤干后干刷刷地形成好几道条条，有的像极薄的吉野纸粘在上边。我想饭和汤既然都已做好，就满可以给我吃嘛。在这种时候，客气是毫无意义的，即使不能如愿以偿，反正也没有什么亏可吃，不如我干脆催一下我的早饭，尽管我在这个家里是只白吃闲饭的猫儿，饥饿毕竟还是一样的。想到这里，我便“喵喵”地向阿三叫了几声，又似撒娇，又似诉怨诉苦，可阿三根本不予理睬。她生来就是犟脾气，不懂人情，这点我是早已领教过的，不过，这就要看我的本领了，必须号叫得好，以便唤起她的同情。于是我又改变了喵喵的叫声为“噢噢”的叫声，连我自己都相信，这种悲泣声带有凄惨之音，足以唤起天涯游子的断肠之思呢。然而阿三却全然不顾。也许这女人是个聋子。聋子是干不了厨娘差事的，很可能她只对猫的叫声是聋的。据说世上有所谓色盲的人，本人自以为具有正常的视力，可医生却说是个残废。这个阿三大概是声盲吧。声盲当然也属于残废。别看她残废，却十分蛮横，在深夜里，不管我怎样要撒尿，请她给我开门，她从来没有给我开过。偶尔她放我出去，却又再也不肯放我进来。即便是夏天，那夜里的露水也是于身体有害的，更何况深秋之严霜。我在屋檐下整夜伫立，等待日出，其茹苦含辛，真是常人无法想象的。

paragraphs.source_en: The other day, when she shut me out, I was attacked by stray dogs and very nearly lost my life; fortunately I managed to climb onto the roof of the shed, where I spent the entire night trembling. All these misfortunes are the evil consequences of Osan's lack of compassion. With someone like her, no matter how piteously one begs, there is no hope of any response. Still, just as people say one prays to the gods when hungry, poverty lowers the spirit, and the sight of a girl makes one want to write a love letter, in such circumstances one tries appealing to her anyway. On my third yowl, in order to attract her attention, I deliberately produced a more complicated cry. I was confident that this exquisite sound was no whit inferior to a Beethoven symphony, but it still seemed to have no effect whatever on Osan. Osan suddenly bent her knees, lifted the floorboard over the indoor storage pit, and took out a piece of hard charcoal about four inches long; she struck it against the corner of the brazier and broke it into three pieces, blackening the area with charcoal dust, some of which seemed even to fly into the soup. Osan was not a woman to concern herself with such things, and immediately pushed the three broken pieces of charcoal into the brazier beneath the pot. It appeared she would never appreciate my symphony. Having no choice, I was quietly about to return to the sitting room, and as I passed beside the bath area, the household's three little girls were in the midst of washing their faces and making a great commotion.
